title: The Queenship of Mary (22 August)
hookLine: a week after the Assumption, Mary honored as queen

cards: A week ago the Church kept the Assumption: Mary, taken body and soul into heaven. In the rosary, the very next glorious mystery, the last one, is a coronation.

It turns up in paintings and stained glass: gold, stars, and a crown lowered onto Mary's head by her Son. Yesterday's crown sat on a king. Today's sits on a woman from a small town who married a carpenter.
So why call her a queen at all? And what kind of queen would she be?

teach.b: Start with the Gospel. Before Jesus is born, the angel tells Mary about her son, in the Douay-Rheims: "and of his kingdom there shall be no end." A king.

Catholics reason from that in one short step: the mother of the king is the queen. When Mary visits her cousin, Elizabeth greets her: "whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?"
Second, the old kingdom of Israel.

teach.h: THE KING'S MOTHER AT HIS RIGHT HAND.
teach.b: When Bathsheba comes to her son, King Solomon, he rises to meet her and has a throne set for the king's mother, "and she sat on his right hand." And she came to ask a favor for someone else.
Catholics read Mary in that seat: not ruling in her Son's place, but near him, bringing other people's requests.
Third, the Apocalypse, the Bible's last book: "a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars."
Readers have heard Israel in that woman, or the Church; Catholic tradition also hears Mary. Fourth, what kind of queen. Catholic teaching is careful here.
Mary is not a goddess. She is a creature, like everyone else, honored because of her Son.

teach.h: A MOTHER'S CROWN, NOT A GODDESS.
teach.b: Her crown is a mother's crown.
That's why the old hymn, the Salve Regina, greets her as queen and, in the same breath, as mother of mercy. The two titles explain each other.
Other Christians honor Mary in other ways, and some don't use this title at all.

how: On 22 August Catholics keep the memorial of the Queenship of Mary; Catholics pray the Salve Regina, one of the Marian antiphons that can close Night Prayer, and the last glorious mystery of the rosary is her coronation.

o: a Latin grace said before a family meal
an old hymn greeting Mary as queen and mother
the Latin blessing said at the end of Mass

games.q: you're King Solomon on your throne. your mother walks in to ask a favor for someone else. what do you do?
o: stay seated and hear her out.
rise to meet her, and set a throne for her at your right hand.
have her wait with the rest of the court.
games.why: he rose to meet her and had a throne set for the king's mother, "and she sat on his right hand." Catholics read Mary's place in that seat.

practice: If you pray and know the Salve Regina, pray it slowly from its opening words, Hail, holy Queen, with a breath between the lines; if you don't know it, hold its first two titles side by side, Queen and Mother, and notice which feels far away and which feels close.
If you don't pray, bring to mind someone who has authority over you and still treats you like family, and hold them in mind with thanks.

wordCard.voice: Salve Regina, the old hymn greeting Mary as queen. The Queenship of Mary is the feast, a week after the Assumption, that honors her as queen because she is the mother of the King.

orig.note: Latin: queen. the Salve Regina opens by greeting Mary with this word.
